entries.modern_form: PIE *kam-er- / *kh2em-er- 'to bend, curve; vaulted' (Pokorny 524-525) with the nasal extension *kam-p- 'to bend' (Pokorny 525); Walde-Pokorny set it up as *qam- (qem-?) 'wölben, biegen', 'perhaps only with the r-formant: qamer-'
entries.note: Every one of Nourai's five root labels is a real reconstruction taken from his own sources. Pokorny p.524-525 has 'kam-er-: to bend, curve, vaulted' (material: Skt. kmarati, Av. kamarā, Gk. kamára, Lat. camur(us)) and p.525 'kam-p-: to bend' (Skt. kampate, Gk. kampē, Lat. campus, Goth. hamfs, Lith. kampas), with Pokorny's own remark that 'kamp- is possibly an extension from *kam- "bend, curve"'. The variants 'Qam, Qem' are Klein's notation for the same base (Klein s.v. camera: 'fr. I.-E. base *qam-, *qem-, "to bend, vault"'), and Walde-Pokorny I 349 heads the article 'qam- (qem-?) "wölben, biegen"'. Language label ('Indo-European') and gloss ('to bend, also a cavity, vault') are therefore both correct. The cross-reference to 'Gěu 1: to bend' is Nourai's own; Pokorny keeps geu- 'bend, curve' (p.393 ff.) apart from kam-, and no modern source merges them. The weak links on this chart are not the root but three of its branches: Old Persian (#4), Germanic heaven (#12) and, to a lesser degree, Latin campus (#14).

nodes.derivation: Avestan kamarā- f. 'belt, girdle' (Yasna/Vendidad usage; the girdle later ritualised as the kustīg) is the standard Iranian witness for PIE *kam-er- 'to bend, vault': a *kam- 'bend' + -er- stem, semantically 'the thing that goes round / the encircling band', with the secondary sense '*vault' inferred by Fick and repeated by Pokorny and Walde-Pokorny. Nourai's gloss 'waist, belt, also a vault' reproduces Pokorny's 'belt, girdle (and "*dome")' word for word. Not to be confused with the homophonous Av. kamarəδa- 'head (of daevic beings)', which Bartholomae (Airan. Wb. 440) and Hübschmann keep separate; Nourai correctly does not import it.
nodes.derivation_fa: واژهٔ اوستایی kamarā- «کمربند، شال کمر» (همان بندی که بعدها در آیین زردشتی «کُستی» شد) گواه اصلی ایرانیِ ریشهٔ هندواروپایی *kam-er- «خمیدن، طاق‌زدن» است: ستاک *kam- به‌همراه پسوند -er-، با معنای آغازینِ «آنچه گرداگرد چیزی می‌پیچد». معنای دومِ «طاق، گنبد» را فیک بازسازی کرده و پوکورنی و والده‌ـ‌پوکورنی همان را آورده‌اند؛ پس شرحِ نورایی «کمر، کمربند و نیز طاق» درست است. این واژه را نباید با kamarəδa- اوستایی به معنی «سرِ دیوان» یکی گرفت؛ بارتولومه و هوبشمان آن دو را جدا می‌دانند و نورایی نیز آن را نیاورده است.

nodes.derivation: kamar «کمر» 'waist, belt' is the regular continuant: Av. kamarā- > Old Iranian *kamarā- > Middle Persian kamar (MacKenzie, Concise Pahlavi Dict. p.50: 'kamar [kml | N ~] waist; belt, girdle. ~-band [-bnd] belt') > NP kamar, with the compound کمربند kamar-band already Middle Persian. Wiktionary (after Edelman, ESIJa IV 191) gives exactly this chain and adds Manichaean MP qmr /kamar/ 'vault', so that the Persian word carries the 'arch, cupola, arched bridge' sense too — which is why the Persian entry can also mean 'the middle of a mountain'. kamrâ «کمرا» 'high-ceilinged room, stable' is weaker: Hübschmann, Pers. Stud. no.867 (p.88) calls np. kamra 'Gewölbe, Stall' a LOANWORD ('np. LW. kamra', after Nöldeke) beside Arm. kamar 'Gewölbe' = Gk. kamára = Lat. camera, and says the relation of all this to np. kamar is 'mir unklar'; Mo'in's footnote 9 to Borhan p.1694 says the same — Manichaean Pahlavi kmr' 'طاق، گنبد', Armenian and Persian kamara 'از آرامی' — while adding that the Aramaic is itself from Persian kamar. So kamrā is at best a doublet re-imported through Aramaic/Greek, not a straight descendant of Av. kamarā-, and the single arrow of the chart flattens that.
nodes.derivation_fa: «کمر» دنبالهٔ منظمِ اوستایی kamarā- است: ایرانی باستان *kamarā- ← فارسی میانه kamar (مکنزی ص ۵۰: kamar «کمر، کمربند»، kamar-band) ← فارسی نو کمر؛ ترکیب «کمربند» نیز از دورهٔ میانه به‌جا مانده است. در فارسی میانهٔ مانوی صورت qmr به معنی «طاق» هم آمده، و از همین‌روست که «کمر» معنای «طاق، گنبد، میانهٔ کوه» هم دارد. اما دربارهٔ «کمرا» (اتاق بلند، طویله) هوبشمان در «مطالعات فارسی» بند ۸۶۷ آن را وام‌واژه می‌داند (کنار ارمنی kamar، یونانی kamára، لاتینی camera) و پیوندش را با «کمر» ناروشن می‌خواند؛ حاشیهٔ معین بر برهان قاطع ص ۱۶۹۴ (پانوشت ۹) نیز آن را «از آرامی» می‌داند، هرچند می‌افزاید که آرامی خود از «کمرِ» فارسی گرفته است. پس «کمرا» بیشتر دوگانه‌ای است که از راه آرامی/یونانی بازگشته، نه بازماندهٔ مستقیم اوستایی؛ ادعای نورایی دربارهٔ «کمر» درست و دربارهٔ «کمرا» با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: Not a direct loan from Persian into English but the classic Anglo-Indian route: Persian کمربند kamar-band 'loin-band' passed into Hindustani/Urdu کمر بند (Urdu kamar first attested c.1635), and British residents in India picked it up in the 17th c. — first recorded in English 1616 as 'combarbands'. Hobson-Jobson s.v.: 'CUMMERBUND, s. A girdle. H. from P. kamar-band, i.e. "loin-band". Such an article of dress is habitually worn by domestic servants, peons, and irregular troops.' The variant kummerbund is only a different transliteration of the same Urdu word (Klein: 'kummerbund, n. — See cummerbund'). AHD's appendix files it under kamer- (waist) and bhendh- (band), which is precisely the two halves of the compound.

nodes.derivation: Neither form is attested Old Persian. Kent's Old Persian lexicon has kamna- 'few', kāma- 'desire', kan- 'to dig' — no kanpa and no čam (grep of KNT.txt); the Achaemenid corpus simply does not contain them. 'kanpa' is Nourai's own back-formation from the nasal-infix family Pokorny lists under kam-p- (Skt. kampate, Gk. kampē, Lith. kampas), i.e. a Proto-Indo-European/Proto-Iranian *kamp-, not an Old Persian word; Cheung's Iranian verb dictionary does set up a root *kamp 'to bend' but its witnesses are Parthian nkmb- 'to bend', Sogdian nk'np-, Chorasmian m|'kfs-, never Old Persian. 'čam' is likewise a Proto-Iranian root, attested in Parthian čm- 'to walk, move to' (Cheung *čam 'to walk'), and Abolghasemi (FFD p.48) derives NP چمیدن from 'پهلوی اشکانی čam < ایرانی باستان *čam' — Old Iranian, i.e. the common ancestor, not Old Persian. Its meaning in the sources is 'to walk/move', not 'to bend'. The node's NOTE comparing Av. xumba 'bent' is separate: Bartholomae's xumba- is a jar/pot word, and Mo'in's footnote to Borhan p.768 links it to خنب/خمب, not to kam-.

nodes.derivation: Four of the five words belong here; one does not. (a) čap «چپ» 'left' is the textbook case: Walde-Pokorny I 350 and Pokorny 525 cite it under kam-p- itself — 'die nasallose gleichbedeutende Sippe von ai. cāpa- "Bogen", capala- "unstet", np. čap "link", d.i. "*krumm"' — and Wiktionary (2026) derives it from PIE *kep- 'to bend', 'a possibly dialectal combination of *kh2emp- + *(s)kamb-', cognate with Skt. cāpa- 'bow', capala-. (b) čapeh «چپه» 'turned over' is the same stem with the adjectival -a(h). (c) čafteh «چفته» 'bent, vaulted' is listed by Cheung under his Iranian root *kamp 'to bend' ('NP čaftah "curved, bent, a vaulted roof"'), and Borhan (p.620 ff.) treats چفت/چفته in the same family. (d) xam «خم» 'a curve' with خمیدن/خماندن: Horn, Grundriss no.446 (p.99) puts it explicitly in this root — 'Zu derselben Wurzel wird übrigens auch np. xam, xamm (*xamp) ... "krumm, gebogen", xamīdan etc. gehören' — beside čap (no.435) and Gk. kamptō, kampylos; the x- for expected k- is what makes the word irregular and is why Horn reconstructs *xamp. Borhan p.768 defines خم as 'ضد راست است که کج باشد ... و کجی و چفتگی چیزها را نیز گویند'. (e) čamīdan 1 «چمیدن» glossed 'walk flauntily' is the disputed one: Cheung splits the material, giving 'NP čamidan "to twist, bend"' to *kamp but 'NP čamidan "to walk proudly"' (with Parthian čm-, Bal. čamit) to a separate root *čam 'to walk' which 'does not have an IE origin and may be a blend of *čar(H) and *gam', and Abolghasemi p.48 derives چمیدن from Parth. čam < Old Iranian *čam 'to run/walk'. Borhan p.661 does give چمیدن both senses ('خرامان راه رفتن ... و بپیچیدن و خم شدن هم آمده است'), which is how Nourai (and Horn's tradition) came to file the 'walk' verb here; but on the modern view the strutting verb and the bending verb are homonyms from different roots. The extras چمبر/چنبر 'hoop' are supported: Horn no.446 derives čanbar (phlv. čambar 'head-fillet') from the same root as čap.

nodes.derivation: kamára 'vaulted chamber, covered wagon, four-poster' is the Greek member of kam-er- and is beyond dispute (Pokorny 524, WP I 349, Mann kamoros, Klein s.v. camera); Herodotus already has kamárē. Two caveats. (i) Fick and others suspected the Greek word of being an Iranian culture-loan (WP I 349: 'wo auch über iran. Lehnformen im gr. Kulturkreis'), and Solmsen proposed a Carian origin — both mentioned and both rejected by Pokorny/WP for the Latin forms at least, so 'inherited cognate' remains the majority view. (ii) kaminos is much weaker: it means 'oven, furnace, kiln', NOT 'fire' as the chart glosses it, and Pokorny admits it only with reservation ('at most kaminos "oven"; certainly this could have derived from a culture word'), while WP I 349 adds that a connection with Slavic kamy 'stone' (i.e. the *ak-/kem- 'stone' root) is 'erwägenswert'. Watkins's AHD entry kamer-, which is the reference cited here, lists kamára only and no kaminos. Klein, however, does state that kamára 'is rel. to kaminos (whence L. caminus)'.
nodes.derivation_fa: kamára یونانی «طاق، اتاق طاق‌دار، ارابهٔ سرپوشیده» عضو بی‌چون‌وچرای این ریشه است (پوکورنی ۵۲۴، والده‌ـ‌پوکورنی ج۱ ص ۳۴۹، مان، کلاین)؛ هرودوت صورت kamárē را دارد. دو نکته: نخست آنکه فیک این واژه را وام‌واژهٔ ایرانی در حوزهٔ فرهنگی یونان می‌دانست و زولمزن ریشهٔ کاریایی برایش پیشنهاد کرده بود، ولی رأی غالب همان هم‌ریشگی است. دوم آنکه kaminos معنایش «تنور، کوره» است نه «آتش»، و پوکورنی آن را «دست‌بالا» به این ریشه می‌بندد و می‌افزاید که ممکن است واژه‌ای فرهنگی و مهاجر باشد؛ والده‌ـ‌پوکورنی پیوند آن را با kamy اسلاوی «سنگ» شایستهٔ درنگ می‌داند و واتکینز در AHD (همان مأخذی که نورایی گواه گرفته) زیر kamer- تنها kamára را آورده است. پس این خانه با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است و معنای «آتش» برای kaminos نادرست است.

nodes.derivation: Both Latin words are straightforward borrowings from Greek, as the chart draws them. Ernout-Meillet: 'camera, -ae f. (camara ...): toiture voûtée, voûte ... Emprunt latinisé au gr. kamára. Classique, usuel'; and 'caminus, -i m.: four. Emprunt au gr. kaminos, correspondant au lat. fornax. Terme technique, fréquent surtout dans la langue de l'Église et dans les langues de métiers (potier, forgeron)'. Latin camera then feeds the whole Romance family (It./Sp./Cat. camera/cámara, Fr. chambre, OHG chamara, OCS komora, Lith. kamara, OIr. camra — Klein). Pokorny notes that beside the loan Latin also has an inherited cognate camur(us) 'arched, crooked', which is why the borrowing did not feel foreign. Nourai's gloss of caminus as 'hearth' is right for the classical use (Vergil's caminus = forge/hearth).

nodes.derivation: chambre is impeccable: Latin camera > Vulgar Latin *camra > Old French chambre (with the regular Gallo-Romance ca- > cha- palatalisation and the intrusive -b- in the -mr- cluster), attested since the 11th c. cabaret is the loose link: it is not a French continuation of camera at all but a re-import — French cabaret 'tavern' (13th c.) was borrowed from Middle Dutch cabret, itself denasalised from cambret / Old Picard camberete, a diminutive of Picard cambre (= chambre), so 'little room'. Klein: 'cabaret, n. — F., a loan word fr. MDu. cabret, denasalized fr. cambret, camret, fr. OPicard cambrete, dimin. of cambre, "chamber, room"'; Etymonline is more cautious ('of uncertain origin, perhaps from Middle Dutch cambret ...'). So the ultimate source is indeed Latin camera, but the arrow Latin > French hides a Picard-Dutch detour and a diminutive suffix.
nodes.derivation_fa: «chambre» بی‌عیب است: camera لاتینی ← لاتینی عامیانهٔ *camra ← فرانسوی کهن chambre، با دگرگونی منظمِ ca- به cha- در گالوـ‌رومی و افزودن «b» میان m و r. اما «cabaret» پیوند سست این خانه است: این واژه دنبالهٔ مستقیم camera در فرانسه نیست بلکه واژه‌ای بازگشته است؛ فرانسوی cabaret «میکده» (سدهٔ ۱۳م) از هلندی میانهٔ cabret گرفته شده که خود از cambret و آن از پیکاردی کهن camberete، مصغّرِ cambre (= chambre) یعنی «اتاقک» است. کلاین همین را می‌گوید و اتیمولوجی‌آنلاین محتاطانه‌تر «ریشهٔ نامطمئن، شاید از هلندی میانه» می‌نویسد. پس سرچشمهٔ نهایی همان camera لاتینی است، ولی پیکانِ «لاتین ← فرانسه» یک چرخش پیکاردی‌ـ‌هلندی و یک پسوند تصغیر را پنهان کرده است.

nodes.derivation: A 20th-century French loan, taken in with the other Parisian entertainment vocabulary (رستوران، بوفه، شامپاین) during and after the Qajar-era contact with France; the ending -eh renders French final -et as pronounced [ɛ], exactly as in بوفه/کاباره/کروکه. Mo'in's dictionary registers it, and the 2-volume abridgement glosses it 'کاباره: میکده، میخانه، مشروب‌فروشی'. Nothing Iranian about the word itself — it is the far end of a loop that started with Greek kamára, so the chart's placement is correct.

(L.) L. camera, a chamber; hence camera obscura, a dark chamber, box for photography; see Chamber.' chimney reaches English through French: Latin caminus 'hearth, forge' > Late Latin (camera) caminata 'room provided with a fireplace' > Old French cheminee > Middle English chimenee > chimney (Klein s.v. chimney; Skeat s.v. Chimney). The chart's single Latin > English arrow therefore telescopes an Old French stage for chimney, but the Latin source is correct for both words.

nodes.derivation: The forms are real — Proto-Germanic *himinaz / dissimilated *hibin- 'heaven' (Goth. himins, ON himinn, OS/OHG himil, OE heofon) — and the gloss 'the vault (of heaven)' is a fair paraphrase; but no modern authority derives them from kam-er-, and Nourai's own reference contradicts him. Watkins/AHD, which is the reference cited on this node, puts *himin-, *hibin- under the root ak- 'sharp': 'suffixed form *ak-men, stone, sharp stone used as a tool, with metathetic variant *ka-men ... b. *ke-men- (probable variant) in Germanic *himin-, in dissimilated form *hibin-, "the stony vault of heaven", in Old English heofon: HEAVEN. [Pok. 2. ak- 18, 3. kem- 556.]' — i.e. the two forms the chart quotes are lifted from the ak- article and reattached to the wrong root. Walde-Pokorny I 350 explicitly warns against this node: 'got. himins usw. "Himmel" braucht nicht als "Gewölbe" benannt zu sein, sondern kann als "*Deckender" ... zu kem- "bedecken, einhüllen" gehören', and adds that *qamer- can only be set up 'wenn himins, cumera (und kaminos) ausscheiden'. Klein s.v. heaven likewise: 'These words prob. derive fr. Teut. base *hama(n)-, fr. I.-E. base *kem-, *kam-, "to cover"' — his 'to cover' base, not the *qam-/*qem- 'to bend, vault' base of his camera article. The current consensus (Kroonen, followed by Wiktionary) derives *himinaz from PIE *h2eḱmō 'stone (sky as a stone vault)', gen. *h2ḱmnós, cf. Skt. aśman, Gk. akmōn; the *ḱem- 'cover' proposal of Frisk and Kluge is the runner-up. Nourai was probably misled by Klein's bare cross-reference 'Cp. also heaven' at the end of the camera entry.

L. campus ... fr. I.-E. base *qamp-, "to bend"'. Two reservations keep this from 'confirmed': Watkins's AHD appendix, one of the two references cited here, restricts kamp- to the Greek forms (kampē, kampylos) and does not list campus at all; and Ernout-Meillet give campus a full article with no Indo-European etymology whatever, treating it purely as a Latin-Romance item. Campania is the regular adjectival derivative (campanius/campaneus 'of the open country' > Late Latin campania 'plain'), the name of the plain around Naples — Klein s.v. campaign: 'L. Campania, name of a province of Italy about Naples, lit. "the plain or level country"'. That much is exactly Klein, KLN p.266-267. The second half of the chart's gloss conflates two words: the French province and the wine are Champagne (Klein: 'champagne, n. — F., abbreviation of vin de Champagne, "wine made in the province of Champagne", a name derived fr. Late L. campania'), which is the same Late Latin etymon but a proper name with its own spelling; the common noun champaigne 'open country' has nothing to do with wine. Nourai has fused the two entries of his own source into one box.

Two qualifications: the immediate source is the proper name Champagne / vin de Champagne, not the common noun champaigne 'open country' drawn as the parent; and Nourai's English gloss 'Champaign' is the wrong word for the wine (English champagne).

nodes.derivation: All three go back to Latin campus, as drawn, though by three different roads. champaign 'open country' is straight from Old French champaigne (Klein p.266). champion is Middle English from Old French champion < Late Latin campiō, -ōnem 'fighter', literally 'one who takes the field' — the Frankish-Latin term for a judicial duellist in the campus (Klein: 'champion, n. — ME., fr. OF. champion, fr. Late L. campionem, acc. of campio, "fighter", lit. "one who takes the field", fr. L. campus, "field"'). camp is the odd one out: it did not come through Old French but was taken in the 16th c. from Italian campo / French camp (military sense), and Skeat thinks it may even be direct from Latin — 'Camp. (L.) We find F. camp (Cot.); but the E. word was prob. taken directly from L. campus, a field, ground held by an army.' Note that Klein's own camp article stands on p.226, not on p.266 as cited, though he cross-refers to champaign from there.

nodes.derivation: Two things to separate. (1) The transliteration: the printed page (pdf p.237, image saved as sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/237.png) really does read 'capân' for «کپان» — a bare c that Nourai's own system never uses for ک (he writes kamar, kâbâreh, and marks the affricate as č in čap, čamîdan). The extraction is faithful; the misprint is the book's, and the form should read kapân (variants قپان qapân, قبان qabbân, colloquial Tehrani قپون qapun). (2) The etymology is essentially right but the route is compressed. Persian کپان/قپان is a steelyard, a one-pan balance; Wiktionary derives it 'from Byzantine Greek κάμπανος (kámpanos), γάμπανος, from Latin campāna' — the campana, the balance named after Campania, the very link the chart's node #14 supplies ('name of an area in Italy famous for its scales'). What the chart's direct Latin > Persian arrow hides is the Byzantine Greek stage and the Syriac/Arabic transmission: Asbaghi (PLA p.216) lists Arabic قبان qibbān 'Schnellwaage' with 'pers. کپان kapān' and a Syriac form beside it, and Tobia al-Unaysi has 'قبان ـ فارسي «كپان» وهو ميزان للأحمال الثقيلة'; Mo'in's entries کپان and قبان cross-refer to each other as mo'arrab/original. Persian and Arabic lexicography therefore treat کپان as the source of Arabic qabbān, whereas the Greco-Latin origin makes the Persian word itself a borrowing — probably through Aramaic/Syriac qanpānā. The Ferdowsi verse of the chart ('به کپان درم سختن آغاز کرد') shows the word already in Persian by the 10th c.
nodes.derivation_fa: دو چیز را باید جدا کرد. نخست آوانگاری: در صفحهٔ چاپی (تصویر در sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/237.png) به‌روشنی «capân» آمده است، حال آنکه نورایی خودش «ک» فارسی را همه‌جا k می‌نویسد (kamar، kâbâreh) و «چ» را č؛ پس این خطای چاپی کتاب است نه خطای خوانشِ اسکن، و صورت درست kapân است (گونه‌ها: قپان، قبان، و در گفتار تهرانی قپون). دوم ریشه‌شناسی که در اصل درست ولی فشرده است: «کپان/قپان» ترازوی یک‌کفه‌ای است و ویکی‌واژه آن را از یونانی بیزانسی kámpanos و آن را از campāna لاتینی می‌گیرد — همان «ترازوی کامپانیایی» که خانهٔ شمارهٔ ۱۴ نمودار به شهرتِ کامپانیا در ترازو اشاره می‌کند. آنچه پیکانِ مستقیمِ «لاتین ← فارسی» پنهان می‌کند مرحلهٔ یونانی بیزانسی و انتقال سریانی/عربی است: اصباغی (ص ۲۱۶) عربی «قبّان» را «Schnellwaage» می‌داند و آن را از «فارسی کپان» می‌گیرد و در کنارش صورت سریانی می‌آورد؛ طوبیا العنیسی نیز می‌نویسد «قبان ـ فارسي «كپان» وهو ميزان للأحمال الثقيلة»؛ و معین در دو مدخل «کپان» و «قبان» آن‌ها را معرّب یکدیگر می‌خواند. یعنی فرهنگ‌نویسی فارسی و عربی کپان را سرچشمهٔ «قبّان» عربی می‌دانند، حال آنکه خاستگاه یونانی‌ـ‌لاتینی نشان می‌دهد خودِ واژهٔ فارسی هم وام‌واژه است، احتمالاً از راه آرامی/سریانی qanpānā. بیت فردوسی («به کپان درم سختن آغاز کرد») نشان می‌دهد واژه در سدهٔ چهارم هجری در فارسی جا افتاده بوده است.

Both entries define the one-pan steelyard and tag each other as the mo'arrab form.
